To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a deep learning approach to predicting incident myocardial infracton using harmonized EHR does not provide a substantial improvement over a baseline logistic regression model using established risk factors.
deep learning methods did not provide a significant advantage over standard machine learning methods for the prediction of incident MI in a large EHR dataset.

the deep neural network (DNN) with random undersampling provides superior classification compared with the other methods and that the benefit of the DNN is only moderate, showing a 9.2% increase in F1 Score and 3.4% increase in Area Under Curve (AUC).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of incident myocardial Infarction (MI).
the application of machine learning techniques to the task of identifying patients at risk of MI.
the development of prediction algorithms for MI using deep learning and machine-learning techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of DNN for MI risk prediction using EHR data does not appear to be warranted at this time, given that the performance of the baseline logistic regression model was adequate, and the additional complexity of the DNN models did not provide a substantial benefit.

the use of DNN in this setting does not appear to provide any additional benefit compared with a logistic regression using only known risk factors for MI, despite the large number of features available for training.
DNNs are not yet ready for use in clinical practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNNs do not provide a significant benefit in the prediction of MI, compared to a simple baseline model using only established risk factors.
deep learning may be useful in the prediction of cardiovascular events, but only when trained on a large dataset with a sufficient number of events of interest.
the deep learning model is not superior to traditional machine learning models, and both of them are not superior to logistic regression models using known risk factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of deep learning methods for risk stratification in EHR data is not straightforward and requires careful consideration and evaluation of the results.
machine learning methods are not likely to provide substantial benefit in the near term when applied to harmonized EHR datasets for MI, compared to traditional approaches.
the benefit of machine learning models may be limited in this setting.
